ground: The praise in 1:2 continues: God, already named Lord of the worlds and the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving, is now called the Owner (mālik; in the other canonical reading, the King, malik) of the Day of Dīn. Yawm al-dīn is the Quran's fixed name for the Day of recompense and reckoning, when each is repaid for what they did. This is the last of the third-person descriptions before the speakers turn to address God directly in 1:5.

triggers.how: The branches of one root (obedience B001, reckoning B002, debt B003, subjugation B004, habit B005, entrusting B007) read together as facets of one concept
shared scene rule.obedience / rule.ownership: the service owed is named in the next ayah

findings.statement: The Day of Dīn is the Day of recompense, and the root beneath dīn names one relation seen from several sides: being bound under another's claim, owing, obeying and being held to it, and in the end having it returned to you. So the Day is where the whole relation comes due.
findings.perceptible: In Turkish, 'din' means a belief system, and 'Din Günü' sounds like 'the day of religion'. The Arabic word ties obedience, debt, habit and repayment into one bond between someone who owes and the one who holds the claim. The Day is when that bond is closed out. The same word the reader knows as 'religion' names what is owed and what is paid back.

triggers.how: shared scene time.age: yawm as a fixed term or appointed time (B002, B005), and a debt in the dictionary is 'sale to a fixed term'
B002: the owner of the claim
scene trade.debt: repayment role

findings.statement: The Day of recompense can also be heard as a due date: dayn is a debt 'to a fixed term', the lexicons quote 'dāyantu Arwā wa-l-duyūnu tuqḍā' ('I lent to Arwā, and debts are paid'), and yawm is a set time. The One who owns that day holds every outstanding account.
findings.perceptible: It gives the Day a time structure the reader can feel. It is not a vague 'end' but a term that has been running all along and arrives on schedule. Everything done before it counts as a running balance.

triggers.how: the dictionary proverb 'kamā tadīnu tudān' uses the same verb in active and passive
favor given and returned, the plan's image I7 of gift and return

findings.statement: Recompense in dīn is mirror-shaped. The proverb 'kamā tadīnu tudān' ('as you deal, so you will be dealt with') uses one verb for the act and for its return. So the Day of Dīn is the Day on which each person's own dealing comes back to them.
findings.perceptible: The judgment has a reciprocal, almost physical shape: the same motion goes out and comes back. It is not a penalty added from outside. The Turkish 'ceza' (penalty) cannot carry this.

triggers.how: two mutawatir readings: mālik (Ḥafṣ, Kisāʾī, Yaʿqūb, Khalaf) and malik (Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Shuʿba, Ḥamza)
scene rule.kingship / rule.ownership: rabb is both owner and king

findings.statement: Mālik (owner, the one who holds and disposes, B002) and malik (king, the one who commands and rules people, B003) are both canonical. The Lord of the Day is at once the one to whom it belongs and the one who rules in it.
findings.perceptible: Turkish keeps malik (owner) and melik (ruler) apart as separate words. In the recited Fatiha both stand on the same letters: ownership of a thing and rule over people. Al-Rāghib notes that malik is said of ruling people, not things. The two readings together cover the Day itself and those who stand in it.

triggers.how: the owned object is a stretch of time

findings.statement: Mālik is an active participle joined to 'day'. Al-Azharī explains it as 'yamliku iqāmata yawmi al-dīn' (He owns the bringing-about of the Day). Al-Rāghib reads malik as 'King on that Day', citing 40:16, 'Whose is the kingship today? God's.' So what is owned is a time itself, and the owning reaches into a Day not yet come.
findings.perceptible: The reader normally thinks of owning things. Here the thing owned is a day: its coming, its timing and what happens in it are in one hand. The participle construction, which lexicographers read with a verbal sense, lets the ownership point forward in time.

triggers.how: parallel genitive construction: rabbi l-ʿālamīn / māliki yawmi l-dīn
space and populations against a single time

findings.statement: Rabb of the worlds and mālik of the Day are parallel titles of ownership. The first spreads across everything that exists, the second over one decisive time, so the praise names God's possession of all space and then of the end of time.
findings.perceptible: The shape of the opening becomes visible: two ownership titles bracket the mercy titles, one spatial (worlds) and one temporal (a Day). The reader sees that nothing, neither place nor moment, falls outside the owner addressed in 1:5.

triggers.how: immediately preceding: the mercy titles stand between Lord and Owner of the Day
same

findings.statement: The Owner of the Day of recompense is named immediately after the All-Merciful and the Mercy-Giving. The one who holds the account is the same one already named twice for womb-mercy.
findings.perceptible: The order of words sets the tone of the Day: the creditor is introduced to the reader first as merciful. The due date belongs to someone whose mercy has already been stated. This does not remove the reckoning; it tells the reader whose reckoning it is.

triggers.how: scene rule.ownership: servant, servitude
B002: al-mamlūk is the ʿabd; the dictionary glosses al-madīn as al-ʿabd

findings.statement: Dīn also names subjugation and service: al-madīn is the bondsman, al-madīna the bondswoman, 'as if work had humbled them'. So the Day of Dīn is also the Day on which the service owed by the owned ones is weighed by their Owner.
findings.perceptible: It prepares the turn in 1:5. Mālik, madīn and ʿabd form one household vocabulary of owner and owned, so 'You alone we serve' reads as the owned ones' answer to hearing whose Day it is.

triggers.how: scene ritual.prayer / divine.lordship: worship
scene: al-dīn al-qayyim is a Quranic collocate

findings.statement: Across most of the Quran (73 of 92 uses) dīn is the way of obedience people follow. Inside 'the Day of recompense' that sense stays audible: this is the Day on which the obedience people kept, or did not keep, is answered.
findings.perceptible: It joins the Turkish reader's 'din' (religion) to the Day instead of cutting it off. The way one follows now and the account one meets then are the same word at two points in time.

triggers.how: the dictionary gives 'mā zāla dhālika dīnī wa-dīdanī', my habit
B002 duration: a life's span of days

findings.statement: Dīn is also habit, one's settled custom (daʾb). The Day of recompense is the Day on which what each person habitually did, day after day, is gathered and answered.
findings.perceptible: The reckoning is not only of dramatic deeds but of repeated daily conduct. The 'days' of a life add up into one Day.

triggers.how: the entry cites 'al-kayyisu man dāna nafsahu wa-ʿamila li-mā baʿda l-mawt' ('the shrewd one is he who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death')
present-tense service

findings.statement: The verb of dīn can also take the self as object (dāna nafsahu, held himself to account). The Day of Dīn has a counterpart now in the person who settles their own account before it falls due.
findings.perceptible: The Day reaches back into the present: someone who keeps accounts with themselves is already living toward it. That is exactly the posture the speakers take in 1:5.

triggers.how: yawm used for the great event that comes down; ayyām as momentous events (B004)

findings.statement: Yawm is a day of daylight, and also the momentous event that 'comes down', like the ayyām of the Arabs (their battles and calamities). The Day of Dīn is therefore both a date and an event that strikes.
findings.perceptible: Turkish 'gün' and 'yevm' sound like calendar units. The Arabic word also carries the weight of a decisive clash or visitation, so the Day has force and not just a place on a calendar.

triggers.how: concordance: mālik al-mulk, who gives and takes kingship
concordance: people as owners of the livestock God made for them

findings.statement: The lemma mālik occurs only three times. Twice it is God (Owner of the Day, Owner of kingship itself), and once it is humans who own the herds God made for them.
findings.perceptible: The same word names a herdsman's ownership of his flock (36:71) and God's ownership of the Day. That quietly links 1:4 to the surface's herd image: the owned ones of 1:5 stand to their Owner as a flock to its master, and every other owner holds only what was made for them.

triggers.how: scene body.strength: those who seek help lack strength of their own
scene body.strength / dwelling.building: standing upright

findings.statement: The root's first image is holding firm: kneading dough tight (malaktu l-ʿajīn), and 'mā lahu milāk' (he cannot hold himself together). The Owner of the Day is also the one who holds together when the self cannot hold itself.
findings.perceptible: Ownership is felt as grip and cohesion. On the Day no one 'owns' themselves, and the dictionary even says 'mā lahu mawlā milākatin dūna Allāh', that no one ever truly owned him but God. This leads into the plea for help in 1:5.

triggers.how: scene travel.route: road
scene travel.route
scene travel.route: stray

findings.statement: Malk al-ṭarīq is the middle and main course of the road ('stay in the malk of the road'). The same letters as the Owner can be faintly heard beside the road the speakers will ask for in 1:6.
findings.perceptible: It is a faint sound bridge from Owner to road: the main course of a road is called by the owner's root, and straying off it is the danger at the surah's end.

triggers.how: milāk al-amr: that on which a matter rests; 'the heart is the milāk of the body'

findings.statement: Milāk is what a matter rests on and what keeps it in good order, as the heart does the body. The Owner of the Day is also the one on whom that Day, and everything settled in it, depends.
findings.perceptible: Ownership as a structural center: something that bears weight, not only a legal title.

triggers.how: scene pastoral.herding: lead animal
scene pastoral.herding: herd, fold

findings.statement: The lexicons use this root for the lead of a flock or the queen of the bees, the one the rest follow. It can be heard faintly beside the Owner whom the herd follows toward the Day.
findings.perceptible: A small addition to the herd image opened in 1:1: owner and leader of the herd in one word.

triggers.how: scene rule.covenant: oath

findings.statement: Tadyīn is trusting a man's own word in judgment or oath, leaving him to his dīn. On the Day of Dīn that trust is finally tested.
findings.perceptible: The Day as the point where what was left to one's conscience is verified.

triggers.how: plan: ghayr as blood-money
plan: anger that demands redress
plan: blood gone unavenged

findings.statement: The claims vocabulary heard faintly in 1:7 (compensation, anger that demands redress, what goes unavenged) stands under the Day named here. The surah's closing words can be heard as unsettled accounts looking toward their settling day.
findings.perceptible: A link across the surah: 1:4 names the Day, and 1:7 hints at the claims that will meet on it.

triggers.how: māliki is genitive in agreement with li-llāhi
switch to second person immediately after

findings.statement: Māliki is still in the genitive, attached to 'li-llāhi' in 1:2. The whole of 1:2–4 is one continuous sentence about God, and 1:4 is its last title before the speakers turn and say 'You'.
findings.perceptible: Hearing 'Owner of the Day' is what triggers the turn. After naming the One who holds the account, the speakers stop describing and address Him directly.

triggers.how: concordance: 'what will make you know what the Day of Dīn is?'
concordance: denial of dīn tied to how the orphan is treated

findings.statement: In the phrase yawm al-dīn, and in 18 uses altogether, dīn is recompense and accountability, most often something people affirm or deny.
findings.perceptible: The phrase is a fixed Quranic name, and one that is contested: saying it in 1:4 is already taking a side, affirming a Day that others deny.

loaded_words.role: In the fixed phrase yawm al-dīn (and nearby recompense contexts), the Day of recompense and accounting, typically something affirmed or denied (82:9, 83:11, 95:7, 107:1). Elsewhere, the way of obedience people follow.
loaded_words.count: 18 of 92 uses are recompense/accountability; 73 are 'a way people follow'; 1 is the king's law (12:76)
loaded_words.departure: Turkish renderings 'Din Günü' make the reader hear 'Religion Day'. 'Ceza Günü' narrows recompense to punishment. 'Hesap Günü' is closest but loses both the reciprocity ('kamā tadīnu tudān') and the link to obedience and debt.

loaded_words.role: The owner who holds and disposes: God as Owner of the Day and of kingship itself (1:4, 3:26), humans as owners of the livestock made for them (36:71).
loaded_words.departure: 'Sahip' is right but flat, and 'Malik' reads as a legal property term. The other canonical reading, malik (king), is lost in any single Turkish word.

loaded_words.role: Overwhelmingly the time-setting of resurrection, gathering and reckoning.
loaded_words.departure: 'Gün' is a calendar unit. The Arabic also carries the momentous event (B003) and the appointed term (B005).

losses.loses: Reckoning, recompense, debt to a term, subjugation or service, and habit. What remains is the reciprocal bond of claim and return.
losses.adds: A sense of institutional religion or confession, so that 'Din Günü' is heard as 'the day of religion'.

losses.loses: Jazāʾ/dīn is repayment in kind, good or bad. Turkish 'ceza' means only punishment or fine.
losses.adds: A purely punitive tone that makes the Day sound only threatening.

losses.loses: Malik keeps only the legal owner and melik only the ruler. The recited Fatiha keeps both. 'Sahip' loses the grip and cohesion sense (malk, milāk).
losses.adds: 'Malik' adds a deed-and-registry, real-estate feel (mülk, emlak).

losses.loses: The appointed term (due date) and the sense of a momentous event (ayyām as decisive events).
losses.adds: 'Yevm' feels archaic or formulaic, and 'yevmiye' pulls toward daily wages.

losses.loses: 'Hesap' (account) is close but loses 'kamā tadīnu tudān', the returning of one's own dealing, and the link to obedience and debt.

grammar: māliki is genitive, continuing the attributes of li-llāhi from 1:2. 1:2–4 is one sentence about God, and 1:5 switches to direct address.

māliki yawmi l-dīn is a chain of two iḍāfas: the owned object is a day (time), and 'the dīn' defines which day. The lexicographers read the participle with verbal force: He owns the bringing-about of the Day.
variants: mālik (owner; Ḥafṣ, Kisāʾī, Yaʿqūb, Khalaf) and malik (king; Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Shuʿba, Ḥamza) are both mutawatir. Together they give ownership of the Day (al-Azharī: He owns its coming about) and kingship on the Day (al-Rāghib, citing 40:16 'Whose is the kingship today?'). This supports F4 and the household image I4.
reread: After the worlds and the twice-named mercy, the praise reaches a single Day and names God as its Owner, and in the other reading its King. The Day is called by dīn: the bond under which one owes, obeys and keeps a habitual way, and which ends in repayment 'as you dealt, so you are dealt with'. A day in Arabic is both an appointed term and an event that comes down, so this Day is a due date when every running account is settled. God, who owns all space as Lord of the worlds, also owns the end of time. Having named the One who holds their account, the owned ones can no longer speak about Him in the third person, and in the next breath they say 'You alone we serve'.

set_aside.what: م ل ك B009 malak (angel) heard in the same letters
set_aside.why: The dictionary itself derives malak from ʾlk (message), a different root. No word in the neighbourhood activates messengers beyond a weak speech.news scene, and it adds nothing perceptible to the Owner of the Day.

set_aside.what: م ل ك B004 imlāk (marriage contract), scene kin.marriage with ihdinā
set_aside.why: There is no marriage vocabulary in the surah beyond a single scene role. Kept only as an attested branch, with no payoff here.

set_aside.what: م ل ك B007 'our waters are our mulūk' (the water on which travellers depend)
set_aside.why: The waste/stray scene is activated only from 1:1 and 1:7. The image of a water-source owner of the Day is not completed by any word in 1:4–6. Noted for 1:7's stray image if needed.

set_aside.what: د ي ن B006 madīna (the town where the ruler's obedience is enacted)
set_aside.why: The dwelling.settlement scene gives no activation in 1:4 itself. It adds to the Turkish loan 'Medine/medeniyet' but not to the reading of the Day.

set_aside.what: ي و م B001 daylight / noon link with al-mustaqīm (time.day_night scene)
set_aside.why: A Day of full daylight when everything is exposed is not attested as a sense of yawm al-dīn in the entries. It would rest on association alone, so it is not kept as a finding.
